deck: Google’s Cheyenne power agreement highlights the scale of Western electricity demand. Farm finances, fuel costs and housing conditions reveal mounting pressures across the region.

signals.headline: Google commits to a $1.8 billion power expansion in Cheyenne
signals.body:
Black Hills Corp. signed definitive agreements October 6 to supply Google's planned Cheyenne data center, advancing one of Wyoming's largest new electricity projects. Black Hills plans to invest $1.8 billion in 564 megawatts of natural gas generation and manage another 2.1 gigawatts of contracted resources through a private microgrid. Electricity service is scheduled to begin in late 2027, with demand reaching its planned peak in 2030.

The financial arrangements are as consequential as the investment. Google has agreed to bear the costs associated with serving the data center, including protections against shifting those expenses to existing utility customers. Black Hills expects the agreements to generate approximately $150 million in annual net income by 2030.

Wyoming is attracting a new category of industrial electricity demand, supported by its energy resources and available land. The agreement provides a test of whether large technology investments can finance their own infrastructure while generating economic activity for surrounding communities. The protections are contractual; their effectiveness will ultimately depend on implementation.

signals.headline: USDA announces a record $13.8 billion in farm payments
signals.body:
USDA announced October 7 that its Agriculture Risk Coverage and Price Loss Coverage programs will generate approximately $13.8 billion in gross payments for the 2025 crop year, the largest annual total since the programs began in 2014. The payments cover crops including corn, wheat, soybeans and grain sorghum, which underpin much of the Plains agricultural economy.

The following day, USDA announced another $1.8 billion in Conservation Reserve Program payments for 2026. That program compensates landowners for conservation practices, including maintaining grassland used for grazing. Nearly 1 million new acres were accepted into Grassland CRP this year.

The payments provide substantial income support as producers contend with weak crop prices and elevated operating costs. The $13.8 billion figure is before statutory payment limits and sequestration, while the conservation payments cover a separate program year. The combined announcements show the scale of federal support flowing into agriculture, although the distribution across Western and Plains states requires further accounting.

source.label: USDA Farm Service Agency · Agriculture Risk Coverage and Price Loss Coverage

additionalSources.label: USDA Farm Service Agency · Conservation Reserve Program

signals.headline: Oil outlook rises $14 a barrel, even as pump prices ease
signals.body:
The U.S. Energy Information Administration raised its fourth-quarter Brent crude forecast to $105 per barrel on October 6, $14 above its September projection. The agency expects Middle Eastern supply disruptions to persist through year-end. Two days later, Hurricane Isaias forced the shutdown of approximately 1.3 million barrels per day of Gulf of Mexico oil production, adding another disruption to an already strained market.

Western fuel prices remain particularly uneven. In the week ending October 5, national regular gasoline fell 11.1 cents to $4.35 a gallon, while California rose another 3.8 cents to $6.23. Diesel eased nationally to $6.20, but remained at $7.23 on the West Coast and $8.08 in California.

The latest forecast suggests expensive fuel could persist even if recent production disruptions prove temporary. The higher costs favor oil producers in New Mexico, Wyoming and North Dakota, while weighing on transportation, agriculture and household spending elsewhere. Western gasoline and diesel markets also face their own refining and distribution constraints, leaving regional prices unusually sensitive to disruptions.

source.label: U.S. Energy Information Administration · October Short-Term Energy Outlook

additionalSources.label: U.S. Energy Information Administration · Weekly Fuel Prices

signals.headline: Record farm debt may be higher than official estimates
signals.body:
U.S. farm debt has climbed above $605 billion, a record, but new reporting suggests farmers may owe substantially more than official statistics capture. An October 8 Reuters investigation found that borrowing from equipment dealers, agricultural suppliers and other nontraditional lenders is increasingly difficult for USDA to track. Previous research involving Kansas State University found that some categories of equipment debt were as much as four times larger than official estimates indicated.

A separate October 6 Purdue University survey found farmer sentiment fell from 135 to 123 in September. A record 52% of respondents identified rising input costs as their greatest concern, while expectations for long-term farmland values reached a record high.

The findings raise questions about financial conditions across the Plains. Farmers remain optimistic about the value of their land while expressing growing concern about operating margins. Meanwhile, lenders may have an incomplete picture of total borrowing. USDA is now studying the extent of nontraditional agricultural credit, with implications for how policymakers assess financial stress in rural economies.

additionalSources.label: Purdue University/CME Group Ag Economy Barometer

signals.headline: Data centers could claim nearly two-thirds of Nevada's electricity sales
signals.body:
Eight data-center companies, including Microsoft, Amazon and Switch, have intervened in NV Energy's long-term electricity planning process, according to reporting published October 6. The utility's projections show data centers increasing from approximately 5% of electricity sales today to 64% by 2046.

The forecast is part of NV Energy's integrated resource plan, filed in May and now undergoing regulatory review. It depends on substantial future development that has yet to materialize. The companies' participation gives them a formal role in proceedings that will help determine how Nevada accommodates growing electricity demand.

The scale of the projection has implications for existing customers. Serving large new loads requires generation, transmission and other infrastructure, raising questions about how those costs are allocated. Nevada and Wyoming are approaching similar pressures from different positions: Wyoming has just announced a major agreement with explicit customer-cost protections, while Nevada is weighing how to serve a potentially much larger share of electricity demand from data centers.

signals.headline: Las Vegas home prices fall $20,000 from their spring peak
signals.body:
Southern Nevada's median existing single-family home price fell to $470,000 in September, according to data released October 6 by Las Vegas REALTORS. Prices are now $20,000 below their May and June record of $490,000, although they remain unchanged from September 2025. Single-family home sales declined 7.4% from a year earlier, while the number of homes listed without an offer rose 6.6%.

Financing conditions worsened further this week. Freddie Mac reported October 8 that the national average 30-year fixed mortgage rate climbed to 7.40%, up from 7.28% the previous week. The increase extends a sharp rise in borrowing costs that has constrained home purchases across the West.

Las Vegas offers a concrete example of how the housing market is adjusting. More homes are available, sales have slowed and prices have retreated from their peak. Yet the increase in financing costs continues to offset some of the affordability benefit for buyers. The changing balance between supply, demand and mortgage rates will determine how much further the market adjusts.

signals.headline: South Korea disputes a proposed $54 billion Alaska gas investment
signals.body:
A proposed $54 billion South Korean investment in Alaska's long-planned natural gas project remains unsettled. President Trump defended the announcement October 2 after South Korean officials indicated that no final commitment had been made. The investment was presented as part of a larger $200 billion package of South Korean projects in the United States.

Alaska LNG would connect North Slope natural gas reserves to an export facility near Nikiski through an approximately 800-mile pipeline. The project has been under consideration for decades, but its enormous construction costs have repeatedly complicated financing. Its developers argue that Alaska's proximity to Asian buyers would reduce shipping costs enough to support the investment.

The proposal could significantly expand Alaska's energy industry and generate substantial construction activity. Its economics remain dependent on securing financing, customers and commercially competitive delivered gas prices. The reported $54 billion is proposed investment rather than committed capital, leaving the project's ultimate scale and timetable unresolved.

signals.headline: Trump announces diesel-tax relief as harvest costs mount
signals.body:
President Trump signed an executive order October 5 in Grand Island, Nebraska, temporarily expanding access to red-dyed diesel fuel, normally reserved for agricultural and other off-road uses. The order allows broader highway use and directs Treasury to defer the associated federal excise tax through December 31 without interest or penalties.

The relief comes as diesel prices remain exceptionally high. Nebraska had already introduced its own temporary program allowing qualifying agricultural transporters to claim refunds of state fuel taxes. Together, the measures are intended to reduce costs for farmers and truckers during a period of unusually expensive fuel.

The economic relief may be limited. The federal order defers tax payments rather than permanently eliminating the underlying obligation, and the federal diesel excise tax amounts to 24.4 cents per gallon. The larger problem remains the cost and availability of diesel itself. With global supplies constrained, temporary tax relief may provide some cash-flow benefits without substantially changing what producers and freight operators ultimately pay.

signals.headline: Microsoft and Adobe lose access to a major green-card program
signals.body:
The Trump administration announced October 8 that Microsoft, Adobe and several major technology services companies would be suspended from the federal permanent labor certification program. The program allows employers to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards after demonstrating that hiring them will not adversely affect American workers.

The Labor Department said it would stop accepting new applications and processing pending applications involving the named companies. Administration officials alleged abuses of the system, while Microsoft defended its hiring and compensation practices. The action does not automatically revoke workers' existing H-1B visas, but it restricts an important route to permanent residency.

The decision is particularly relevant to Washington and California, where major technology employers depend on specialized international labor. Its consequences could extend to recruitment and employee retention, although the immediate effects on regional hiring remain unclear. The suspension arrives as Western technology companies continue investing heavily in AI infrastructure despite relatively weak broader employment growth.

signals.headline: Federal energy lease sales generate nearly $400 million in one quarter
signals.body:
The Bureau of Land Management reported October 8 that federal oil, gas and geothermal lease sales generated nearly $400 million in receipts during the third quarter of 2026. Oil and gas sales accounted for $372.1 million, covering offerings across New Mexico, Wyoming, Colorado, Montana and the Dakotas, Nevada, Utah and other areas.

Geothermal leasing contributed another $25.8 million. Utah accounted for nearly $24.7 million through an August sale covering more than 72,000 acres, while an Oregon sale generated another $1.1 million. The activity reflects continued industry interest in Western subsurface energy resources, including geothermal development.

Lease receipts represent an important revenue source for federal and state governments, with portions distributed according to applicable revenue-sharing arrangements. They also provide an indication of demand for development rights. The receipts themselves are upfront leasing revenue, however, rather than production income, and do not establish that the leased parcels will ultimately produce energy. Future drilling, project development and royalties will determine the longer-term economic returns.
